content: Benzonatate is an antitussive medication approved by the FDA for the symptomatic relief of cough. It is commonly associated with adverse reactions such as nausea, oral hypesthesia, throat symptoms, numbness, dizziness, headache, sedation, and somnolence. Adult Indications and Dosage For adults, the usual dose of benzonatate is 100 mg or 200 mg taken orally three times daily (tid). If necessary to control cough, the dose may be increased to a maximum of 600 mg per day, divided into three doses. Benzonatate capsules must be swallowed whole and should not be broken, chewed, dissolved, cut, or crushed. Pediatric Indications and Dosage For children over 10 years of age, the dosing is the same as for adults: 100 mg or 200 mg orally three times daily. The maximum daily dose is 600 mg, divided into three doses. As with adults, the capsules must be swallowed whole and not altered in any way. Contraindications Benzonatate is contraindicated in individuals with hypersensitivity to benzonatate or related compounds. Warnings 1. Hypersensitivity Reactions: Severe hypersensitivity reactions, including bronchospasm, laryngospasm, and cardiovascular collapse, have been reported. These reactions may occur if the capsule is chewed or dissolved in the mouth, leading to local anesthesia. Severe reactions may require intervention with vasopressor agents and supportive measures. 2. Psychiatric Effects: Isolated cases of bizarre behavior, including mental confusion and visual hallucinations, have been reported, particularly when benzonatate is taken with other prescribed drugs. 3. Accidental Ingestion and Death in Children: Benzonatate must be kept out of reach of children. Accidental ingestion has resulted in death in children under 10 years of age. Symptoms of overdose can appear within 15-20 minutes, and death has been reported within one hour of ingestion. Immediate medical attention is required in cases of accidental ingestion. Adverse Reactions Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include: Hypersensitivity Reactions: Bronchospasm, laryngospasm, cardiovascular collapse, potentially related to local anesthesia from chewing or sucking the capsule. Central Nervous System (CNS): Sedation, headache, dizziness, mental confusion, visual hallucinations. Gastrointestinal (GI): Constipation, nausea, GI upset. Dermatologic: Pruritus, skin eruptions. Other: Nasal congestion, burning sensation in the eyes, vague chilly sensation, numbness of the chest, hypersensitivity. Overdose, whether deliberate or accidental, has resulted in death, particularly in children. Use in Specific Populations 1. Pregnancy: Benzonatate is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and it is unknown whether benzonatate can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. 2. Nursing Mothers: It is unknown whether benzonatate is excreted in human milk. Caution is advised when administering to nursing women. 3. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness in children under 10 years of age have not been established. Accidental ingestion in children under 10 has resulted in death. 4. Geriatric Use: There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of benzonatate in elderly populations. 5. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of benzonatate in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Administration and Monitoring Benzonatate capsules must be swallowed whole. They should not be broken, chewed, dissolved, cut, or crushed. The FDA package insert does not provide specific information regarding drug monitoring. Overdosage Overdose of benzonatate, whether intentional or unintentional, can result in death, particularly in children. Signs and symptoms of overdose may appear within 15-20 minutes and include CNS stimulation (restlessness, tremors, clonic convulsions) followed by profound CNS depression, convulsions, coma, cerebral edema, and cardiac arrest. Death has been reported within one hour of ingestion. Treatment involves immediate medical attention, gastric evacuation, administration of activated charcoal, and intensive support of respiratory and cardiovascular-renal function. CNS stimulants should not be used. Pharmacology Benzonatate acts peripherally by anesthetizing stretch receptors in the respiratory passages, lungs, and pleura, thereby dampening their activity and reducing the cough reflex at its source. Its effects begin within 15-20 minutes and last for 3-8 hours. Benzonatate does not inhibit the respiratory center at recommended dosages. Storage Benzonatate capsules should be stored at controlled room temperature (20° to 25°C or 68° to 77°F) and protected from light, moisture, and humidity. Patient Counseling Information Patients should be instructed to swallow benzonatate capsules whole and not to break, chew, dissolve, cut, or crush them. If the capsule is released in the mouth, it can cause temporary local anesthesia of the oral mucosa, which may lead to choking. Patients experiencing numbness or tingling of the tongue, mouth, throat, or face should refrain from oral ingestion of food or liquids until the numbness resolves. If symptoms worsen or persist, medical attention should be sought. Benzonatate must be kept out of reach of children due to the risk of fatal accidental ingestion. Brand Names Benzonatate is marketed under the brand names Tessalon Perles and Zonatuss.
